topics.title: Chapter 28 — Locality
topics.summary: Locality is a pattern of reuse. Temporal locality concerns returning to the same information, while spatial locality concerns accessing nearby information. Hardware caches and software buffers exploit these patterns by retaining recently useful data and moving adjacent bytes together. Locality is not a property of a data structure in isolation. It depends on the traversal and workload. The same matrix can be accessed in a cache-friendly or cache-hostile order, and the same linked structure can behave differently when nodes are allocated compactly rather than scattered.

topics.title: 28.1 Temporal locality
topics.summary: Temporal locality occurs when an item used now is likely to be used again soon. A loop repeatedly updating a small set of accumulators exhibits it. Retaining those values in registers or cache avoids repeated access to slower levels. “Soon” must be interpreted relative to competing accesses and capacity. Reusing an item after touching millions of unrelated bytes may be too late for a small cache. Reuse distance—the intervening distinct data relevant to a cache model—is often more informative than elapsed time alone.

topics.title: 28.2 Spatial locality
topics.summary: Spatial locality occurs when an access predicts accesses to nearby bytes. A sequential array traversal typically uses several elements from each fetched cache line. Fetching an entire line is valuable when the remaining bytes are consumed before eviction. Spatial proximity is not automatically useful. A structure containing many rarely used fields can force frequently used fields to share lines with irrelevant data. A layout that groups the fields used together may reduce transferred bytes without changing the logical records.

topics.title: 28.3 Working sets
topics.summary: A working set is the collection of data and instructions actively used during a relevant phase or interval. Its size and access order determine pressure on caches, TLBs, and physical memory. Different phases of one program can have different working sets. A useful analysis chooses a time scale: one inner loop, one request, one batch, or a steady-state interval. Counting every allocation in the process may overestimate the hot working set, while counting only explicit input arrays may omit indexes, metadata, code, and thread stacks.

topics.title: 28.4 Sequential access
topics.summary: Sequential access follows adjacent locations in a predictable order. It can use most bytes of each cache line and allow hardware prefetching to anticipate future accesses. It also often reduces translation pressure by consuming many bytes within each page. The benefit depends on actual use. Reading a large array once still incurs compulsory traffic. Sequential order makes that traffic efficient; it does not make the bytes free. Streaming too much unrelated data can also evict useful cached state.

topics.title: 28.5 Strided access
topics.summary: Strided access advances by a fixed distance between elements. Small strides may retain useful spatial locality; large strides may touch a new line or page for every item. Particular stride patterns can also interact poorly with cache-set indexing. When analyzing a stride, express it in bytes. A stride of 16 elements means 64 bytes for four-byte elements but 128 bytes for eight-byte elements. Element count without element size does not determine cache-line use.

topics.title: 28.6 Random access
topics.summary: Random access uses an order that is difficult to predict from recent addresses. It can reduce prefetch usefulness and increase the number of distinct lines or pages needed for a small amount of useful data. Randomness should be defined carefully: a random permutation of a compact array differs from pointers distributed across a much larger heap. A benchmark should generate its access order outside the timed region when the goal is to measure memory traversal rather than random-number generation. It should also preserve dependencies intentionally: independent random loads and dependent pointer chasing test different limits.

topics.title: Worked example — Row-major versus column-major traversal
topics.summary: Assume a row-major 64 × 64 matrix of eight-byte elements and 64-byte cache lines. A row contains 512 bytes, or eight lines. Traversing a row consecutively uses eight elements from each line before moving on. A column traversal advances by 512 bytes between successive elements. It touches one element in each of 64 different rows before returning to the next element of the first row. If the relevant cache cannot retain those lines, much of each fetched line is wasted before reuse. If it can retain them, the difference may be smaller. Capacity and associativity determine the result; “column traversal always misses” is too strong. A blocked traversal processes a smaller rectangle before moving elsewhere. For example, an 8 × 8 tile contains 512 bytes of element data. In a transpose or matrix operation, choosing tiles whose active input and output regions fit the useful cache budget can preserve reuse. Include all simultaneously active arrays and temporary storage when estimating the budget.

VERBATIM GRADUATE LECTURE TRANSCRIPT
Charles Dorner

SLIDE 1: Chapter 28 — Locality

LECTURE NARRATION
Locality is a pattern of reuse. Temporal locality concerns returning to the same information, while spatial locality concerns accessing nearby information. Hardware caches and software buffers exploit these patterns by retaining recently useful data and moving adjacent bytes together. Locality is not a property of a data structure in isolation. It depends on the traversal and workload. The same matrix can be accessed in a cache-friendly or cache-hostile order, and the same linked structure can behave differently when nodes are allocated compactly rather than scattered.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION

SLIDE 16: Worked example — Row-major versus column-major traversal

LECTURE NARRATION
Assume a row-major 64 × 64 matrix of eight-byte elements and 64-byte cache lines. A row contains 512 bytes, or eight lines. Traversing a row consecutively uses eight elements from each line before moving on. A column traversal advances by 512 bytes between successive elements. It touches one element in each of 64 different rows before returning to the next element of the first row. If the relevant cache cannot retain those lines, much of each fetched line is wasted before reuse. If it can retain them, the difference may be smaller. Capacity and associativity determine the result; “column traversal always misses” is too strong. A blocked traversal processes a smaller rectangle before moving elsewhere. For example, an 8 × 8 tile contains 512 bytes of element data. In a transpose or matrix operation, choosing tiles whose active input and output regions fit the useful cache budget can preserve reuse. Include all simultaneously active arrays and temporary storage when estimating the budget.
